title: Bài báo ngắn
text:
LOCAL BAKERY RISES TO NATIONAL FAME

Greenhill (May 22) — Just five years ago, Rosa Delgado was selling bread from a single stall at the Greenhill farmers' market. Today, her company, Rosa's Oven, supplies more than 300 supermarkets across the country.

The turning point came in 2023, when a food blogger's video about her sourdough loaf attracted two million views in a week. "Overnight, we had more orders than we could bake," Ms. Delgado recalled. "I had to decide: stay small or grow fast."

She chose growth — but carefully. Rather than opening her own factories, she partnered with three family-run bakeries in nearby towns, training their bakers in her methods. This allowed production to triple while keeping the handmade quality that made her famous.

Rosa's Oven will open its first overseas location in Singapore this fall. Asked for her advice to small business owners, Ms. Delgado laughed: "Make something worth talking about. The talking, these days, takes care of itself."

title: Bài báo: xu hướng văn phòng
text:
THE QUIET RETURN OF THE OFFICE LIBRARY

Business Trends Weekly (October issue) — Five years ago, office designers could not knock down walls fast enough. Open floor plans promised collaboration, spontaneity, and — not least — lower costs per desk. Today, a growing number of companies are quietly rebuilding what they tore down, one bookshelf at a time.

The newest feature in workplace design is the "library zone": a carpeted, phone-free room where conversation is limited to a whisper. At software firm Datawheel, the library seats thirty and is booked solid by ten each morning. "Our engineers asked for it by name," says workplace director Irene Kovacs. "They didn't want more meeting rooms. They wanted somewhere to think."

Research supports the shift. A 2025 university study tracking 1,200 office workers found that those with access to designated quiet areas reported 23% fewer errors in detail-heavy tasks and, perhaps surprisingly, rated their teams as MORE collaborative — not less. The authors suggest that when deep-focus work has a protected home, meetings become shorter and more purposeful.

The trend has its skeptics. Retrofitting quiet rooms is expensive, and some managers worry the spaces simply hide employees from oversight. But with several major insurers and two government ministries announcing library zones this quarter, the whisper, it seems, is getting louder.

title: Bài báo: giờ làm 4 ngày/tuần
text:
FOUR DAYS, FULL PAY: LOCAL FIRMS JOIN THE SHORTER-WEEK EXPERIMENT

Harbor City Business Journal — When Meridian Insurance announced last spring that its 300 employees would work four days a week for the same salary, competitors predicted chaos. Eighteen months later, the company reports its strongest customer-satisfaction scores in a decade — and its lowest staff turnover ever.

Meridian is not alone. According to a survey by the Harbor City Chamber of Commerce, one in five local employers now offers some form of compressed schedule, up from one in twenty just three years ago. The catch? Success appears to depend less on the calendar than on the meeting room. "Companies that simply squeezed five days of meetings into four failed quickly," says labor researcher Dr. Elsa Moreau. "The ones that thrived cut internal meetings by half or more before touching the schedule."

Not every industry finds the shift easy. Restaurants, hospitals, and logistics firms — where customers expect seven-day service — must hire additional staff to cover the gaps, an expense small businesses cannot always absorb. Meridian's chief executive, Priya Raman, acknowledges the model has limits, but she is blunt about the results in her own office: "We measure output, not hours. Output went up."
